content: Intermittent preventive treatment (IPT) is recommended for pregnant women living in regions where malaria is endemic because it provides significant health benefits for both the mother and the baby. However, the effectiveness of this approach may differ in HIV-positive pregnant women, as HIV infection compromises the immune system, potentially altering the response to malaria prevention strategies. The objective of this study was to compare different IPT regimens for malaria in HIV-positive pregnant women residing in malaria-endemic areas. To achieve this, a comprehensive search was conducted in June 2011 across multiple databases, including the Cochrane Infectious Diseases Group Specialized Register, CENTRAL, MEDLINE, EMBASE, LILACS, and the metaRegister of Controlled Trials (mRCT). Additional information was sought from reference lists, conference abstracts, researchers, and organizations involved in relevant trials. The study included randomized controlled trials that compared various IPT regimens for preventing malaria in HIV-positive pregnant women in malaria-endemic regions. Data extraction and risk of bias assessment were performed by two authors. Dichotomous outcomes were analyzed using risk ratios (RR), while continuous outcomes were assessed using mean differences (MD), both with 95% confidence intervals (CI). Two randomized trials were included in the analysis, involving a total of 722 HIV-positive pregnant women from Malawi and Zambia. Both trials compared a monthly regimen of sulfadoxine-pyrimethamine (SP) to the standard two-dose regimen administered during the second and third trimesters of pregnancy. Among women in their first or second pregnancy, monthly SP appeared to reduce maternal parasitemia (two trials, 463 participants; RR 0.25, 95% CI 0.14 to 0.43; low-quality evidence) and placental parasitemia at delivery (two trials, 459 participants; RR 0.38, 95% CI 0.21 to 0.70; low-quality evidence). The monthly SP regimen may have a modest effect on reducing maternal anemia at delivery (two trials, 447 participants; RR 0.93, 95% CI 0.72 to 1.20; low-quality evidence) and the number of babies born with low birth weight (two trials, 469 participants; RR 0.80, 95% CI 0.52 to 1.23; low-quality evidence). However, larger trials are needed to confirm or refute any clinically significant benefits for these outcomes. There is currently insufficient evidence to determine whether monthly SP has an impact on neonatal mortality (one study, 253 participants; very low-quality evidence). For women in their third or higher pregnancy, the evidence is insufficient to draw any conclusions about the benefits of monthly SP compared to the two-dose regimen (one trial, 166 participants; very low-quality evidence). Additionally, no trials were identified that evaluated other IPT regimens for HIV-positive pregnant women. The authors concluded that administering three or more doses of SP may offer some advantages over the standard two-dose regimen in HIV-positive pregnant women. However, larger trials are necessary to confirm any effects on outcomes that are important to patients. It is important to note that SP cannot be given concurrently with co-trimoxazole, a medication frequently recommended for infection prophylaxis in HIV-positive pregnant women. Therefore, there is a pressing need for the development of new drugs and further research to address the specific needs of this population.
